deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematical derivation. It belongs to Hilbert's notebook of aphorisms and reflections on the nature of mathematics. The previous and next pages are of the same kind. The sentence continues from the previous page: mathematics is not meant to make thinking superfluous. On the contrary, it teaches and trains one to think more than the immediate practical purpose requires.

The points made on the page, in order:

(1) No other science has such beauty, simplicity and lawfulness. Gauss is singled out for the calm, certainty and reliability of his inferences. The truths he found are more lasting than the bronze of monuments, and even than the name Gauss. This echoes Horace's 'aere perennius' and alludes to the Gauss–Weber monument in Göttingen, unveiled in June 1899.

(2) In mathematics one must always connect the two ends of the science: the most modern achievements with the long-known foundations. One climbs mountains to get a better and more comprehensive view of the valleys.

(3) The only quasi-mathematical content concerns formulas and figures. A formula, like a small drawing (as in 'my Gauss-Festschrift'), is a means of intuition. 'My Gauss-Festschrift' is the Grundlagen der Geometrie (1899), published in the Festschrift for the monument's unveiling. Hilbert says his Festschrift makes the rigorous use of such aids possible. His example: instead of the inequality a ≷ b ≷ c (i.e., a<b<c or a>b>c, meaning b lies between a and c), he draws three points a, b, c in order on a line. In modern terms this is the betweenness relation of the order axioms (Axiome der Anordnung, group II) of the Grundlagen. The point is that once the axioms fix the meaning of 'between', the figure can stand rigorously for the formula. Both the written formula and the drawing become merely formal if they are unclear and not fully justified and carefully studied. 'The figure is a drawn formula; the formula is a written figure.'

(4) The arithmetical training (Schule) is necessary, and not only for mathematics.

(5) One should use the sharpest tools and methods as early as possible. Likewise, in modern transport one uses steam railways and electricity even for short distances.

Dating: the reference to the Festschrift and the Gauss monument dates the page to about 1899–1900. This is just before the Paris ICM address, which contains the published version of the formula/figure aphorism.

results.what: Encoding the betweenness inequality a<b<c or a>b>c as a figure of three collinear points a,b,c with b in the middle, justified by the axiomatic treatment in the Grundlagen der Geometrie
results.modern_name: Betweenness relation / order axioms (Pasch–Hilbert axioms of order)
results.usually_credited_to: Moritz Pasch (1882), systematized by Hilbert, Grundlagen der Geometrie (1899)

results.what: Aphorism: 'the figure is a drawn formula, the formula a written figure'
results.modern_name: Hilbert's dictum on geometric figures and arithmetic signs
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert, 'Mathematische Probleme' (Paris ICM address, 1900): 'die Zeichen der Arithmetik sind geschriebene Figuren und die geometrischen Figuren sind gezeichnete Formeln'

results.what: Methodological remarks: connecting the modern frontier with the old foundations; using the sharpest methods early; mathematics trains one to think beyond immediate practical needs; praise of Gauss
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert (similar themes in his 1900 Paris address and later lectures)

deep.surprise_reason: The page holds only aphorisms. Its one mathematical idea, betweenness drawn as collinear points, is the standard content of the Grundlagen. The 'figure = drawn formula' dictum is well known from Hilbert's 1900 Paris lecture. The only mild interest is the draft-stage context linking it explicitly to the Gauss-Festschrift around 1899.

checkable.sympy: from sympy import symbols, And, Or, Q, ask; a,b,c=symbols('a b c', real=True); # check numerically: for many random reals, (a<b<c or a>b>c) == ((b-a)*(c-b)>0)
checkable.asserts: The inequality a ≷ b ≷ c (b between a and c on the real line) is equivalent to (b-a)*(c-b) > 0, which is the arithmetic counterpart of the drawn figure a—b—c.

transcription_corrections: Line 5: 'In keiner Andere Wissenschaft' should read 'In keiner andern Wissenschaft'.
Lines 9–10: probably 'sind nicht nur dauernder als (gewiss) das Erz der Denkmäler, sondern sogar als der Name Gauss'. This is an allusion to Horace's 'aere perennius' and the Gauss–Weber monument.
Line 13: 'mit der altersher bekannten Grundlage' – the parenthesis opened before 'd.h.' is never closed in the manuscript.

Line 15: the interlinear insertion 'Höhen der' (not 'Höhe der') stands above 'bessern'. The intended reading is probably 'eine(n) bessere(n) und umfassendere(n) Blick'. Where exactly the insertion belongs is uncertain.
Line 16: 'Meine Festschrift' appears preceded by a struck-out letter.
Line 18: in 'a ≷ b ≷ c' Hilbert writes a stacked >/< symbol (with a small stroke beneath). The figure shows a line with marks labelled a, b, c in that order.

Line 19: the sentence reads approximately 'Beides, sowohl geschriebene Formel wie Zeichnung, wird formal, wenn unübersichtlich und nicht allseitig gerechtfertigt und genau studirt ist'. The words 'Zeich-'/'wie' are partially struck and repositioned.
Line 23: 'Die Arithmetische Schule' – 'Schule' here means training/discipline.
